full_description: Learn how to organize, query and analyze structured business data using SQL and PostgreSQL—without requiring previous programming experience. This practical SQL & Relational Database Fundamentals course introduces relational database concepts, tables, data types, primary keys, foreign keys and SQL query development. Start by learning to retrieve and filter data using SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, LIMIT and conditional expressions. Develop confidence in combining information across related tables with INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and multi-table queries. Learn to produce business reports using aggregate functions, GROUP BY, HAVING, CASE expressions, subqueries and Common Table Expressions. Explore introductory window functions for ranking and comparing records without losing individual row detail. Build reliable relational databases using CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, constraints and safe INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE operations. Understand transaction fundamentals, database integrity, indexing awareness and the importance of parameterized queries when SQL is used inside applications. Use PostgreSQL with DBeaver or pgAdmin to work on realistic admissions, retail sales or inventory datasets. Complete a portfolio-ready relational database project containing a documented schema, sample data, at least 20 meaningful SQL queries, a data-quality checklist and a business reporting summary. The programme emphasizes practical SQL reasoning, reliable query results, data relationships and business interpretation—not simply memorizing SQL commands.

overview: SQL & Relational Database Fundamentals is an intensive 5-week, 40-hour beginner-friendly certification designed to build practical database and querying proficiency using industry-standard PostgreSQL. Built around modern 2027 data standards, this course teaches complete beginners—without requiring any prior coding experience—to model relational entities, write precise SQL queries, join related datasets, produce actionable business reports, and enforce relational data integrity. Students work with real-world business scenarios (such as student admissions, retail commerce, and warehouse inventory) using professional GUI tools like DBeaver or pgAdmin. Rather than relying on static spreadsheets or slow reporting requests, learning SQL empowers you to extract answers, join customer and transaction data, discover trends, and ensure data integrity independently.

industry_workflow: Business Question Decomposition: Translate operational questions into precise relational data requirements.
Schema Inspection & ERD Navigation: Inspect primary/foreign key relationships to identify correct tables and join keys.
Incremental Query Construction: Build queries step-by-step (FROM -> JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY).
Result Grain & Count Verification: Verify output row counts against raw data to detect accidental row multiplication or filtering errors.
Data Quality Auditing: Check for orphaned records, unexpected NULLs, duplicate business keys, and constraint violations.
Reporting & Handover: Export reproducible SQL script files, document assumptions, and present business insights with supporting query evidence.

Strict Human Validation: Every student must execute their queries in PostgreSQL, verify row counts against raw records, and understand every clause; unverified AI-generated SQL is rejected.
best_practices: Explicit Column Selection: Avoid SELECT * in production and reporting queries; explicitly project only the columns required.
Correct NULL Testing: Never use = NULL or != NULL; always test for missing values using IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
Verify Join Grain: When joining one-to-many tables, understand that parent rows duplicate; reconcile aggregate sums before and after joins.
Safe Modification Workflows: Always test UPDATE and DELETE operations using a SELECT query with the identical WHERE clause before modifying records.
Use Transactions for Multi-Step Updates: Wrap related modifications in BEGIN ... COMMIT blocks, ensuring automatic ROLLBACK on failure.
Enforce Constraints at the Database Level: Use PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints rather than relying solely on applications.
Consistent SQL Formatting: Format SQL with uppercase keywords, clear indentation, table aliases, and descriptive comments for maintainability.
Parameterized SQL Awareness: Never concatenate untrusted user input directly into SQL strings in application code; use parameterized query APIs.
common_mistakes: Using = NULL instead of IS NULL, resulting in false comparison results due to three-valued logic.
Accidental Cartesian products (missing ON clause or join condition), multiplying row counts exponentially.
Using WHERE instead of HAVING to filter aggregated metrics, causing syntax errors.
Double-counting metrics by joining multiple child tables without grouping at the appropriate grain.
Executing UPDATE or DELETE statements without a WHERE clause, inadvertently wiping out entire tables.
Assuming an executed query with zero errors is mathematically correct without reconciling output against raw data.
Using floating-point types (FLOAT/REAL) for monetary values instead of NUMERIC/DECIMAL, introducing rounding errors.
Submitting screenshots instead of executable SQL source files, making work impossible to reproduce and audit.
freelance_applications: Writing custom SQL queries and business reports for small businesses using PostgreSQL or MySQL.
Cleaning and auditing messy operational datasets to identify duplicate records and data errors.
Designing small relational databases and schemas for business workflows, e-commerce, or CRM systems.
Migrating and structuring data from disorganized spreadsheets into normalized relational tables.

modules.title: Database & SQL Foundations
modules.objective: Understand relational database architecture, PostgreSQL setup, SQL language fundamentals, data types, and interface navigation using DBeaver or pgAdmin.
modules.module_purpose: Establish solid conceptual and hands-on foundations in relational databases, distinguishing the database engine from the query language and GUI tools, and creating initial tables safely.
what_you_will_learn: What data is: structured relational tables versus unstructured files and spreadsheets.
RDBMS concepts: entities, tables, rows, columns, and database schemas.
Understanding SQL as the universal relational query language and PostgreSQL as the engine.
Choosing appropriate PostgreSQL data types: INTEGER, NUMERIC/DECIMAL, VARCHAR, TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE.
Setting up PostgreSQL and connecting through DBeaver or pgAdmin.
Executing DDL and DML commands, inspecting result grids, and saving SQL scripts.

lessons.title: Data Concepts & Relational Architecture
subtopics: What is data: structured vs semi-structured vs unstructured information
Why databases replace spreadsheets: concurrency, data volume, integrity, and security
Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) architecture overview
The role of PostgreSQL: history, enterprise adoption, and open-source standards
Understanding the distinction between SQL (the query language) and PostgreSQL (the DBMS engine)

lessons.title: Relational Tables & Data Types
subtopics: Anatomy of a relational table: entities, attributes, rows (records), and columns (fields)
PostgreSQL data types: INTEGER, BIGINT, VARCHAR(n), TEXT, and BOOLEAN
Handling numbers accurately: why NUMERIC/DECIMAL is required for currency instead of FLOAT
Date and time data types: DATE, TIME, and TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE overview
Introduction to Primary Keys as unique entity identifiers and Foreign Keys as relational links

lessons.title: PostgreSQL & Tooling Setup
subtopics: Installing PostgreSQL on your local machine and verifying the background service
Overview of database client interfaces: DBeaver Community Edition and pgAdmin 4
Configuring a new database connection: localhost, port 5432, user, and credentials
Navigating the database object hierarchy: databases, schemas, tables, and views

lessons.title: SQL Language Categories & DDL/DML
subtopics: SQL command categories: DDL (Definition), DML (Manipulation), DQL (Query), DCL/TCL overview
Creating your first table with CREATE TABLE and column definitions
Inserting initial records with INSERT INTO ... VALUES
Running your first query with SELECT * FROM table_name
Reading result grids: inspecting column headers, data types, row counts, and execution times

lessons.title: Query Safety & Database Hygiene
subtopics: Saving and organizing SQL scripts (.sql files) for reproducible workflows
Reading and troubleshooting beginner SQL syntax error messages
Working safely with dedicated local training databases
Data privacy ethics: using fictional business datasets rather than sensitive personal records
Safe SQL workflow checklist before running queries

modules.title: Data Querying
modules.objective: Master data retrieval, projection, compound filtering, sorting, limiting, expressions, and accurate handling of NULL values and missing data.
modules.module_purpose: Learn how to query relational tables with precision, extracting exactly the records and attributes required to answer operational business questions.
what_you_will_learn: Retrieving and projecting data with SELECT, FROM, and column/table aliases.
Filtering rows using comparison operators (=, !=, <>, <, >, <=, >=) and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT).
Advanced filtering with IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, and PostgreSQL ILIKE pattern matching.
Sorting records with ORDER BY (ASC/DESC) and controlling output volume with LIMIT and OFFSET.
Creating calculated fields using arithmetic expressions, string functions, and date math.
Mastering NULL values, three-valued logic, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, and COALESCE.

lessons.title: Basic Data Retrieval & Aliases
subtopics: The SELECT and FROM statement: the cornerstone of relational querying
Why explicit column projection is preferred over SELECT * in reporting
Assigning readable column aliases with the AS keyword
Assigning table aliases to simplify references
Formatting SQL for readability: uppercase keywords, indentation, and comments (-- and /* */)

lessons.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE
subtopics: The WHERE clause: evaluating row-level conditions before returning results
Comparison operators: =, !=, <>, <, >, <=, and >=
Combining conditions with logical operators: AND, OR, and NOT
Operator precedence rules and using parentheses () to avoid logical filter bugs
Filtering with IN and NOT IN for set membership
Range filtering with BETWEEN ... AND ...
Text pattern matching: LIKE wildcards (% and _) and PostgreSQL case-insensitive ILIKE

lessons.title: Sorting, Limiting & Distinct Records
subtopics: Sorting output rows using ORDER BY: ascending (ASC) vs descending (DESC)
Multi-column sorting: primary sort and secondary tie-breaker columns
Restricting result set size with LIMIT to find top records
Pagination concepts: combining LIMIT and OFFSET
Eliminating duplicate result rows using SELECT DISTINCT

lessons.title: Expressions & Calculated Columns
subtopics: Creating calculated fields: arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /) on numeric columns
String operations: concatenation with ||, UPPER, LOWER, and TRIM functions
Date filtering: comparing dates, extracting date parts, and date intervals
Interpreting calculated results in business contexts (e.g., total_revenue = quantity * price)
Checking query row counts to verify filter accuracy

lessons.title: Mastering NULL Values & Missing Data
subtopics: Understanding NULL: the representation of unknown, absent, or unrecorded data
Three-valued logic in SQL: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN
Critical rule: why = NULL and != NULL fail and always evaluate to UNKNOWN
Testing for missing data accurately using IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
Providing default fallback values with the COALESCE(column, default) function
How NULL affects arithmetic calculations and comparisons

modules.title: Joins & Relationships
modules.objective: Model relational database relationships and write accurate multi-table queries using Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, INNER JOIN, and LEFT JOIN without data corruption.
modules.module_purpose: Understand how relational databases connect information across entities, combine related tables, handle unmatched records, and avoid row-multiplication errors.
what_you_will_learn: Relational database design principles: entities, attributes, and relationships.
Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and referential integrity rules.
Relationship types: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many with junction tables.
Writing INNER JOIN queries to combine matching records across tables.
Writing LEFT OUTER JOIN queries to retain unmatched records.
Joining three or more tables across relational hierarchies.
Understanding query grain and preventing accidental Cartesian products.

lessons.title: Relational Modeling & Key Constraints
subtopics: Relational modeling concepts: decomposing flat spreadsheets into normalized tables
Primary Keys: uniqueness, non-nullability, and natural vs surrogate keys
Foreign Keys: establishing links between parent and child tables
Cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many (parent/child), and many-to-many relationships
Modeling many-to-many relationships using junction / associative tables (e.g. Enrollments)
Reading and drawing simple Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERD)

lessons.title: INNER JOIN & Matching Relational Data
subtopics: The purpose of JOINs: combining columns from two or more tables based on related keys
INNER JOIN syntax: SELECT ... FROM table_a INNER JOIN table_b ON table_a.id = table_b.a_id
Using table aliases to qualify columns and resolve ambiguous column name errors
Understanding the result: only rows with matching keys in BOTH tables are returned
Filtering joined data with WHERE clauses and ordering joined outputs

lessons.title: LEFT JOIN & Handling Unmatched Rows
subtopics: The LEFT OUTER JOIN: preserving all records from the left table regardless of matches
How PostgreSQL populates missing child columns with NULL in outer joins
Identifying orphan or inactive records: using LEFT JOIN ... WHERE child.id IS NULL
Deciding when to use INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN for business reporting accuracy
Conceptual overview of RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN

lessons.title: Multi-Table Joins & Complex Queries
subtopics: Joining three or more tables: navigating relationship paths (e.g. Students -> Enrollments -> Courses)
Chaining multiple JOIN clauses in a single SELECT query
Mixing INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN clauses within the same query
Selecting fields across all joined tables and providing clean column aliases
Writing business queries combining customers, orders, order items, and products

lessons.title: Join Accuracy & Row Multiplication
subtopics: Understanding query grain: what single real-world entity does one output row represent?
Why one-to-many joins multiply parent rows (e.g. one order with 3 items produces 3 rows)
The danger of accidental Cartesian products (CROSS JOIN) caused by missing ON clauses
Techniques for verifying row counts before and after joining
Documenting table relationships and join assumptions in project notes

Applying conditional business logic and status tagging with CASE expressions.
Authoring scalar and IN-based subqueries to solve dependent data questions.
Structuring readable, modular queries using Common Table Expressions (WITH clauses).
Applying introductory window functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals).

lessons.title: Aggregate Functions & Reporting Grain
subtopics: Introduction to business reporting: summarizing thousands of rows into actionable metrics
SQL aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX
Critical difference: COUNT(*) (counts all rows) vs COUNT(column) (ignores NULLs)
Using DISTINCT inside aggregate functions: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
Understanding NULL behavior: how aggregates ignore NULLs in numeric calculations

lessons.title: Grouping Data with GROUP BY & HAVING
subtopics: The GROUP BY clause: collapsing rows into summary groups based on shared column values
Grouping by multiple columns: sales by category and year
Rules of grouping: why every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY
The HAVING clause: filtering summary groups after aggregation
Critical distinction: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
Combining JOINs with GROUP BY and HAVING to report on related entities

subtopics: The CASE expression: bringing IF-THEN-ELSE business logic into SQL queries

Categorizing data: assigning status labels (e.g. 'High Value', 'Standard', 'Low')

Correlated subqueries and the EXISTS operator conceptual overview
When to use subqueries vs when to use JOINs or CTEs

Ranking records with ROW_NUMBER() and RANK() to find top items per category
Calculating a simple running total across dates with SUM() OVER (ORDER BY date)

ACID transaction properties and managing transactions with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK.

lessons.title: Safe Record Modifications
subtopics: Inserting data: single-row inserts and efficient multi-row INSERT INTO ... VALUES
Updating records with UPDATE: modifying specific columns with a WHERE clause
Deleting records with DELETE FROM: removing specific rows matching a WHERE condition
The disaster of omitted WHERE clauses: why unconstrained UPDATE/DELETE wipes out entire tables
The mandatory safe modification protocol: run a SELECT with the identical WHERE clause first
Using the RETURNING clause in PostgreSQL to immediately inspect inserted, updated, or deleted rows

lessons.title: Database Transactions & ACID Principles
subtopics: Why transactions are necessary: maintaining consistency across multi-step business operations
Understanding ACID properties: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (rules enforced), Isolation (concurrency), Durability (persisted)
Transaction commands: BEGIN starts a transaction block; COMMIT saves all changes permanently
ROLLBACK: discarding all changes made within the transaction block if an error occurs
Practical transaction scenario: creating a sale and updating warehouse stock atomically

lessons.title: Transaction Rollback & Data Safety

Why application developers must use parameterized queries ($1, $2 or ?) rather than raw string building

faq.question: What is SQL & Relational Database Fundamentals?
faq.answer: SQL & Relational Database Fundamentals is an intensive 5-week, 40-hour practical programming certification course that teaches you to organize, query, and analyze business data using SQL and PostgreSQL. You will learn relational database concepts, table creation, data types, primary and foreign keys, filtering, multi-table joins, aggregations, CASE expressions, subqueries, CTEs, introductory window functions, data integrity, and transactions.

faq.question: Is this SQL course suitable for beginners?
faq.answer: Yes, this course is designed specifically for complete beginners. No prior programming knowledge, computer science degree, or database experience is required. We start with basic data concepts and build step-by-step into writing confident, multi-table SQL queries.

faq.question: Do I need programming knowledge?
faq.answer: No. You do not need to know JavaScript, Python, React, or any other programming language. SQL is a declarative query language that reads similarly to English, making it accessible to anyone with basic computer literacy.

faq.question: What is the duration and course fee?
faq.answer: The course spans 5 weeks with 40 guided learning hours (8 hours per week, consisting of 4 hours of interactive lectures and code-alongs plus 4 hours of hands-on software labs). The course fee is a transparent flat ₹5,900 with zero hidden charges, covering all lectures, labs, code reviews, and certificate verification.

faq.question: Which database will I learn?
faq.answer: You will learn PostgreSQL, the world's most advanced, widely adopted open-source relational database management system. PostgreSQL is the industry standard for production web applications, enterprise systems, and data analytics.

faq.question: What is the difference between SQL and PostgreSQL?
faq.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to communicate with, query, and manage relational databases. PostgreSQL is the actual relational database management system (the software engine) that stores the data, enforces constraints, and executes SQL commands.

faq.question: Will I learn DBeaver or pgAdmin?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn how to connect to PostgreSQL, explore database schemas, write and execute SQL queries, and inspect tabular result grids using professional GUI tools—primarily DBeaver Community Edition and pgAdmin 4.

faq.question: Does the course cover table creation?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn Data Definition Language (DDL) commands, including CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE, selecting appropriate data types (INTEGER, NUMERIC, VARCHAR, TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE), and defining constraints such as PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK.

faq.question: Will I learn SQL filtering and sorting?
faq.answer: Yes. You will master the WHERE clause using comparison operators (=, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, and PostgreSQL ILIKE for pattern matching, as well as sorting output with ORDER BY and restricting rows with LIMIT.

faq.question: Will I learn INNER and LEFT JOIN?
faq.answer: Yes. Combining related tables is a core focus of the course. You will master INNER JOIN to combine matching records and LEFT OUTER JOIN to retain records from the primary table even when no child match exists, understanding how to qualify columns and avoid ambiguous column errors.

faq.question: What are primary and foreign keys?
faq.answer: A Primary Key is a column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a database table. A Foreign Key is a column in a child table that references the Primary Key of a parent table, establishing relationships between entities and enforcing referential integrity.

faq.question: Does the course teach relational database design?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn fundamental relational modeling: identifying entities and attributes, decomposing unstructured spreadsheets into normalized tables, establishing one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships (with junction tables), and reading Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs).

faq.question: Will I learn GROUP BY and HAVING?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn how to aggregate business records using COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX, group summaries by categories or dates using GROUP BY, and filter grouped metrics using the HAVING clause, understanding how it differs from row-level WHERE filtering.

faq.question: Will I learn subqueries and CTEs?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn how to write scalar and list subqueries, as well as Common Table Expressions (CTEs) using the WITH clause. CTEs allow you to break complex, multi-stage business analysis queries into clean, readable, modular blocks.

faq.question: Does the course include window functions?
faq.answer: Yes. You will explore introductory SQL window functions using the OVER clause, PARTITION BY, and ORDER BY. You will use ROW_NUMBER() and RANK() to rank business items and calculate running totals across dates while preserving individual output rows.

faq.question: Will I learn SQL business reporting?
faq.answer: Yes. The course emphasizes practical business analysis: calculating monthly revenue, analyzing customer enrollment velocity, finding low-stock inventory, identifying dormant accounts, and translating business questions into reproducible SQL reports.

faq.question: Will I learn INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands to add new rows (INSERT), modify existing records (UPDATE), and remove records (DELETE). Crucially, you will learn the safe modification protocol: testing with SELECT first to avoid accidental data loss.

faq.question: What are database transactions?
faq.answer: A transaction is a unit of work that bundles multiple SQL operations into an all-or-nothing block. You will learn how BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK guarantee ACID properties, ensuring that if any operation in a multi-step update fails, all changes are safely reversed.

faq.question: Will I learn database constraints?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn how to enforce business rules directly at the database level using PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, and CHECK constraints (such as preventing negative prices or quantities).

faq.question: Does the course cover SQL injection awareness?
faq.answer: Yes. You will learn what SQL injection vulnerabilities are, why concatenating untrusted user input directly into SQL strings creates severe security risks, and why software developers must use parameterized queries when connecting databases to applications.

faq.question: Will I learn advanced PostgreSQL administration?
faq.answer: No. Advanced database administration (DBA) topics—such as replication, failover clustering, WAL archiving, multi-node sharding, and deep kernel performance tuning—are specialized topics outside the scope of this foundational certification.

faq.question: How many SQL queries will I write?
faq.answer: Throughout the course and capstone, you will write dozens of hands-on queries, culminating in a mandatory portfolio requirement of at least 20 distinct, verified business SQL queries covering 20 specific analytical categories.

faq.question: What portfolio project will I create?
faq.answer: You will build the Relational Business Database & SQL Reporting Portfolio—a complete small relational database featuring at least 4 related tables, realistic sample data, 20 verified SQL queries, a 10-point data quality checklist, and an executive business reporting summary.

faq.question: Will I create an admissions, retail or inventory database?
faq.answer: You can choose ONE of three approved business scenarios for your capstone project: Option A (Student Admissions & Enrollment Database), Option B (Retail Sales & Order Management Database), or Option C (Warehouse Inventory Management Database).

faq.question: Will I receive SQL source files?
faq.answer: Yes. You will author and retain complete ownership of all executable .sql source files (create_tables.sql, insert_sample_data.sql, queries_01_20.sql, etc.) along with your README documentation, which you can publish to GitHub as a permanent portfolio.

faq.question: Is this course useful before Node.js backend development?
faq.answer: Yes, it is highly recommended. Understanding relational database schemas, foreign keys, SQL joins, and transactions in Course 59 makes learning database integration in Course 58 (Node.js Backend Development with Express) much faster and more intuitive.

faq.question: Is MySQL also taught?
faq.answer: The course is standardized 100% on PostgreSQL to provide deep, cohesive mastery. MySQL is discussed briefly as an alternative relational database, but all hands-on exercises, queries, and capstone requirements use PostgreSQL.

faq.question: Does the course include data engineering?
faq.answer: No. Large-scale data engineering (Apache Spark, Kafka, Airflow, Snowflake, cloud data lakes) is an advanced discipline outside this foundational course. Course 59 focuses specifically on relational SQL, database design, and business data querying.

faq.question: Is this an official PostgreSQL certification?
faq.answer: This is a Nova Skills institutional certification: 'Nova Skills Certified SQL & Relational Database Associate'. It is not issued directly by the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which does not administer vendor certifications.

faq.question: What entry-level career opportunities are possible?
faq.answer: Graduates are equipped for entry-level and junior roles requiring SQL querying, including Junior SQL Assistant, Junior Data Reporting Assistant, Business Data Assistant, Operations Coordinator, and Backend Development Trainee.
